content: To access the landing page templates, navigate to the Help Menu and select How to Create a Page, or click the provided link. When to Use Landing Pages In cases where a disease entity is extensive or has numerous subtypes with distinct characteristics, it may be beneficial for the author to divide the information into smaller, focused sections. These sections can be presented as individual pages, all of which are interconnected through a central landing page. This landing page provides general information about the disease as a whole. Each of the linked pages would then delve into the specific details of a particular subtype. How to Use a Landing Page All pages linked to a landing page should include hyperlinks directly below their headers. This allows readers to easily navigate to related pages. Some degree of content repetition between pages is expected. Shared information can be reused across pages, along with the appropriate citations. Examples are provided to illustrate different styles of landing pages and their linked pages, such as: A microchapter-style landing page linking to microchapter-style offshoot pages. A single-page-style landing page linking to single-page-style offshoot pages. A single-page-style landing page linking to a combination of microchaptered and single pages. For instance, in the case of colitis, there are multiple subtypes, each with unique epidemiology, risk factors, prognosis, clinical history, symptoms, diagnostic features, and treatment options. This makes colitis an ideal candidate for a landing page with separate chapters for each subtype. In this example, the author has identified eight subtypes of colitis. Three of these subtypes are presented in a single-page format, while five are organized into microchaptered formats. All pages are interconnected and linked back to the main landing page via the headers. Example 1: Pneumonia Pneumonia is divided into two subtypes: Community-Acquired Pneumonia and Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia. These subtypes differ in terms of risk factors, underlying causes, and treatment approaches. The literature discusses these entities separately due to differences in pathogens, microbial resistance, and treatment regimens. To accurately represent this information, the author created a general Pneumonia landing page, along with two microchaptered pages dedicated to each subtype. Example 2: Endophthalmitis Endophthalmitis is another condition with multiple classifications. While the subtypes do not differ significantly from one another, the sheer number of subtypes makes it impractical to consolidate all the information into a single page without overwhelming the reader. To address this, the information is divided into digestible portions, ensuring that high-quality content is delivered in an easy-to-read format. This approach aligns with WikiDoc's goal of providing accessible and well-organized medical information.
